title: Brand tracking tools for scaling companies
content:
Brand tracking tools help growth marketers gauge what people say about the brand, whether it’s good or bad, and why they choose competitors, all at scale. Brand monitoring also reveals AI share of voice and what you should improve to be cited more by LLMs.
However, as with everything in marketing, brand tracking software isn’t a single tool. Brand trackers vary by metrics, AI tracking features, a company’s growth stage, use cases, and pricing.
This post breaks down the differences between brand tracking and brand monitoring, how to choose the best brand tracking tools, like HubSpot AEO, and how to confidently run a brand tracking survey. Let’s dive into the details so you can confidently choose the best-fit brand tracker.
A brand tracking tool is software that measures brand health across channels over time. Modern brand tracking tools collect data from social platforms, search signals, PR coverage, web analytics, customer feedback, answer engines, and brand tracking surveys.
In 2026, the biggest shift is AI visibility. For brand teams, this changes the old workflow. A brand tracker no longer sits only inside quarterly brand perception research. It now integrates survey data, social listening, search demand, AI citations, customer feedback, and CRM reporting into a single decision-making dashboard.
For AI brand tracking, growth teams use HubSpot AEO to monitor how a brand appears across ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Gemini, including AI visibility scores, competitor comparisons, prompt tracking, and citation analysis. With HubSpot AEO, teams clearly understand which sources and content types AI engines cite most.
But before measurement begins, the brand foundation must be clear. Use HubSpot’s Free Brand Building Guide to document positioning, voice, and visual identity before measuring whether the market understands them.
Brand tracking measures longitudinal changes in brand awareness , perception, consideration, preference, and loyalty. Brand monitoring focuses on live detection of brand mentions across the web, social channels, media, forums, reviews, and answer engines. Each solves a different problem:
Continuous listening captures ongoing brand mentions and sentiment shifts between survey waves. A brand tracking survey adds structured feedback that listening tools cannot capture on their own.
Scaling companies, oftentimes, need both to run in parallel. Brand monitoring spots a signal such as a spike in Reddit mentions, for example. Brand tracking proves whether the signal changes market perception. AI brand tracking shows whether answer engines started repeating that narrative when buyers ask for vendor recommendations.
Here is a clear distinction between brand tracking and brand monitoring for decision-makers .
The right brand tracking metrics show how visible, trusted, preferred, and commercially useful a brand has become. These are the core metrics worth tracking first.
Brand strength rarely fails in one place, so all these metrics matter. For example, share of voice can grow because of negative coverage — and marketers definitely want to know this.
HubSpot’s Customer Feedback Software helps revenue teams collect NPS, CSAT, and CES surveys, then view scores, sentiment, and response volume in dashboards. Surveys can be distributed via email or embedded on web pages, creating a smooth experience for your customers.
AI brand tracking measures how often, how accurately, and how favorably a brand appears in AI-generated answers. It tracks whether answer engines mention the brand, which competitors appear in the same responses, which prompts trigger visibility, and which sources shape the answer.
This matters because AI visibility now sits upstream of traffic. A buyer can ask ChatGPT, Gemini, or Perplexity for the best tools in a category and get a shortlist before ever visiting a website. Traditional SEO dashboards cannot fully capture that moment, as the brand can appear in an answer without earning a click. Core AI brand tracking use cases include:
Run HubSpot AEO to see how often your brand appears against competitors across ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Gemini. Your dashboard populates automatically with your brand visibility score, share of voice percentage, and sentiment score.
Brand tracking tools should match the decision the company needs to make. Early-scale teams usually need fast signals and clean dashboards. Mid-market teams need integrations and repeatable reporting. Enterprise teams need governance, multi-market tracking, and research rigor. Before comparing tools, teams should agree on what brand tracking software must help them answer:
Once you’ve written down the answers, it’s easier to map out the list of features that solve your problem. I shortlisted a handful of necessary features for a complex brand health monitoring.
Survey-based tracking measures what buyers think, remember, and prefer. A brand tracking survey captures structured feedback from the audience a company seeks to influence. The tool should support unaided and aided awareness, familiarity, consideration, preference, trust, purchase intent, and brand associations. For B2B companies, it should also support audience filters to capture answers from the real buying committee:
Brand monitoring coverage shows where brand mentions happen outside structured surveys. This includes social media, news, forums, reviews, blogs, podcasts, videos, communities, and AI answers.
Since consumers are increasingly less likely to share feedback directly with companies, that means passive listening and multi-source monitoring are more important for brand health .
AI visibility and share of voice belong in brand tracking now because answer engines influence the shortlist before a buyer reaches a website.
AI visibility shows whether answer engines mention the brand when buyers ask category, comparison, or recommendation questions. AI share of voice measures how often the brand appears in AI-generated answers compared with competitors across the same tracked prompts.
HubSpot AEO is the smartest solution on the market that tracks brand visibility, sentiment, prompt performance, competitor presence, and citations across ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity. It surfaces which sources and content types AI engines are citing in your category, then gives you prioritized recommendations on what to create or improve to increase your share of voice.
Collecting customer feedback belongs to the customer support teams, but separating brand tracking from customer reality is shooting yourself in the foot. A company may improve awareness while customer frustration weakens trust, reviews, referrals, and retention.
Ideally, a brand tracking tool comes with a suite of features for measuring customer satisfaction. Or, you may need to buy and connect a standalone tool.
HubSpot Customer Feedback Software can do all of the above as the tool connects NPS, CSAT, and CES surveys to the customer record inside HubSpot.
The tool should connect brand metrics to CRM data, campaign performance, search trends, social engagement, customer feedback, and web analytics. Only then do growth teams understand what impacts the brand health score and act accordingly.
A strong brand tracking tool should let teams track named competitors across the same audience, markets, channels, and metrics. For AI visibility, this means tracking the same prompts and seeing whether answer engines recommend the brand, competitors, or no vendor at all.
For example, HubSpot AEO tracks selected prompts to analyze how competitor presence in AI answers shifts week over week. Marketers use this data to understand which content types drive the most citations.
A brand tracker should identify themes such as pricing, product quality, customer support, onboarding, integrations, security, ease of use, or brand trust. It should also show whether sentiment is positive, neutral, or negative and whether it differs by channel.
A good brand tracking tool should support role-based dashboards, scheduled reports, permissions, annotations, exports, and clear trend history.
Pricing for brand tracking tools can look simple on the pricing page and become complicated during implementation. Total cost depends on:
Teams should ask vendors to price the actual use case .
One important caveat: Brand teams may not need all features at once, but they should not buy tracking software only to “measure brand” either. The tool needs to show what changed, where it changed, why it likely changed, and what the team should do next.
Brand tracking software is split into three groups: lightweight survey and feedback tools, mid-market listening and AI visibility tools, and enterprise research suites. The best choice depends less on feature volume and more on whether the tool can answer the next business question.
Early-stage teams usually need quick and accurate answers to the three questions: Whether buyers know the brand, what they say about it, and whether AI answer engines include it in their recommendations.
HubSpot AEO is built for marketers who need to know whether their brand shows up when buyers ask answer engines for category recommendations. It tracks visibility across ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity, then shows whether the brand appears, how it compares with competitors, and which sources influence those answers. HubSpot AEO also analyzes AI visibility gaps by showing:
It also turns these gaps into practical recommendations, like updating owned content, building a comparison page, pitching a third-party source, or strengthening social signals.
What I like: HubSpot AEO treats AI visibility as a brand measurement problem and provides a brand visibility score, along with actionable recommendations, all within the same workflow. For lean teams, this cuts the time between “we are invisible” and “this is what we should publish or improve.”
Best for: Growth marketers, brand managers, SEO leads, and revenue teams that need to track AI share of voice and understand why competitors appear in answer engines.
HubSpot Customer Feedback Software helps teams create NPS, CSAT, and CES surveys inside HubSpot’s Service Hub. It works well when brand perception needs customer experience context, especially after support, onboarding, or renewal moments.
HubSpot Customer Feedback Software also connects to the contact, company, ticket, and lifecycle data that explain why the feedback happened. An essential feature for the timely detection of pipeline leaks and appropriate action.
What I like : Feedback sits close to the customer record, which makes it easier to connect poor experience, account risk, and brand perception.
Best for: Customer marketing, CX, and service teams that want to measure how customers feel about the brand after real interactions.
Typeform works well for lightweight brand tracking surveys, campaign recall surveys, message testing, and post-event research. It gives lean teams a clean way to collect structured feedback without buying a dedicated research platform.
What I like: Typeform offers fast, branded surveys where the completion experience matters. It works well for campaign lift questions, message testing, and simple awareness checks.
Best for: Early scale teams that need simple survey collection before investing in a dedicated brand tracker.
Mid-market teams usually look for tools that connect social, search, AI visibility, survey data, and repeatable reporting. They need team workflows and enough integrations to keep brand, growth, and leadership aligned.
Sprout Social is well-suited for teams that need brand monitoring to be closely aligned with social media marketing execution. It combines publishing, scheduling, Smart Inbox, review management, keyword monitoring, reporting, and team workflows.
What I like: Sprout Social is good for social teams that need action and reporting in one place.
Best for: Mid-market social and brand teams that need publishing, monitoring, and executive reporting.
Latana is a dedicated brand tracking platform for teams that need structured survey-based measurement across awareness, consideration, perception, and audience segments. It makes sense when brand leaders need more than ad hoc surveys and want a repeatable view of how the brand performs across markets, competitor sets, and customer segments.
What I like: Lantana offers statistically grounded tracking without having to build a research operation from scratch.
Best for: Scale-ups and mid-market brands that need awareness, consideration, perception, and preference tracking by market.
Brand24 is a brand monitoring and social listening tool for teams that need to track mentions, reach, engagement, sentiment, sources, and influencers across online channels. It fits brands that need broader visibility into where people talk about them, especially across social platforms, news, blogs, Reddit, LinkedIn, Medium, Quora, and YouTube.
What I like: Brand24 has been recommended for a long time and still delivers high-quality social listening data.
Best for: Brand, PR, social, and agency teams that need to track mentions, sentiment, and sources across social and web conversations.
Enterprise teams need stronger governance, broader market coverage, greater historical depth, and reporting that can withstand executive scrutiny. At this stage, brand tracking often informs market strategy, PR planning, category positioning, investor narratives, and budget allocation.
YouGov BrandIndex is an always-on brand tracker with daily tracking across 16 brand health metrics. It covers 56 markets, more than 30 million panel members, and more than 27,000 brands tracked daily. The product is useful when teams need to understand not only whether brand health moved, but also how news, campaigns, or competitor activity affected perception over time.
What I like: The tool is great for competitive benchmarking at scale. Daily tracking helps enterprise teams see whether news, campaigns, or competitor moves changed brand health.
Best for: Enterprise brand monitoring, getting deep insights, and market research.
Talkwalker combines social listening, media monitoring, AI summaries, forecasting, peak detection, and LLM insights. Talkwalker is built for enterprise social listening, media monitoring, and consumer intelligence.
What I like: Talkwalker is good for global brand monitoring because LLM insights now sits beside social listening and media monitoring.
Best for: Enterprise comms, PR, and consumer intelligence teams that need broad media and social coverage listening at scale.
Meltwater offers media intelligence, social listening, consumer intelligence, influencer marketing, real-time alerting, reporting, and GenAI Lens LLM Tracking.
What I like: I like Meltwater for PR heavy teams that need media coverage, social listening, and AI visibility in one vendor relationship. If LLMs rely on specific publishers, journalists, or third-party sources, the team can see where brand narrative work should happen.
Best for: Enterprise PR, communications, reputation, and executive visibility teams that need to understand how media coverage influences AI answers.
Brandwatch is a consumer intelligence and social listening platform for enterprise teams that need to analyze large volumes of online conversation. Its Consumer Intelligence product is built for researchers and analysts who need to search consumer opinion, segment audiences, build customizable dashboards, and analyze data with AI.
What I like: Brandwatch is a great tool for mature research teams needing depth in social data and audience segmentation.
Best for: Enterprise research, insights, social intelligence, and brand teams with high conversation volume and complex reporting needs.
A brand tracking survey is a structured research survey that measures brand health over time. It adds structured feedback that brand monitoring tools cannot capture because most buyers don’t publicly post every opinion that shapes a shortlist.
A good brand tracking survey measures awareness, familiarity, consideration, preference, associations, purchase intent, and competitor comparisons. Here is a practical workflow for designing a brand tracking survey.
Start with the business question. A launch survey might ask whether the campaign increased awareness. A repositioning survey might ask whether buyers now associate the brand with a new category. Every question should connect to a decision someone can act on.
“When you script the survey, give it to people to see and test it. It’s a really important point that cannot be overlooked. We did several iterations on our programming, and with each one, there was an improvement,” shares Daniel Koomson , Senior UX Researcher at News UK .
Sampling should match the market the company wants to influence.
For B2B brand tracking , the sample should reflect the buying committee. That may include job title, seniority, department, company size, industry, geography, buying role, budget authority, and category involvement. For B2C, the sample may depend on age, region, income, category usage, purchase frequency, lifestyle, or brand familiarity.
If the budget is tight, prioritize the most important segment instead of spreading the sample too thin. A smaller but relevant sample beats a larger audience that cannot buy.
A brand tracker needs stable questions across waves. If the team changes the questions every quarter, trend data becomes hard to trust. However, teams can add rotating questions for campaigns, messaging, product launches, new markets, or competitor moves, but keep the core intact.
Unaided questions ask respondents which brands come to mind in a category without showing a list. Aided questions ask whether they recognize specific brands from a list. Unaided awareness should come before aided awareness so that later answers aren’t influenced and inflate recall.
This structure mirrors how buyers move from memory to recognition to evaluation. It also helps teams see where the brand breaks down.
Quarterly works for most scaling B2B companies. Monthly works when paid media, PR, or category competition moves quickly. Daily or weekly tracking usually belongs to enterprise programs with sufficient budgets and sample sizes.
Brand metrics need a competitive context. Awareness, preference, and sentiment mean more when compared against the brands buyers also evaluate.
The competitor list should include direct competitors, category leaders, and any substitute solutions that often appear in sales calls or customer research.
Randomize answer order, avoid leading language, screen for category relevance, and keep competitor lists balanced. Bias often enters brand tracking through wording, order, sample quality, or timing — and it doesn’t always look obvious.
A quick bias check for marketers to run before launch:
If the company just launched a major campaign, earned a viral mention, or dealt with a support issue, annotate the wave. That context helps explain movement later.
Koomson highlighted another major point that can derail your brand teaching survey — it’s captcha: “You want to captcha bots and unplug them to make sure only real new people are answering the survey.”
Survey results should sit beside CRM, traffic, pipeline, campaign, and sales data. This turns brand health monitoring into revenue-linked decision-making. Save the list of signals to compare after each wave:
HubSpot allows growth teams to monitor customer feedback with Customer Feedback Software and AI visibility with HubSpot AEO , both connected to HubSpot’s Smart CRM, so insights sit alongside the customer and contact data that give them context.
Scaling companies should run a brand tracking survey quarterly. Monthly tracking makes sense when the company spends heavily on paid media, enters a new market, changes positioning, or faces fast-moving competition.
HubSpot Customer Feedback Software can run CSAT, NPS, and CES surveys continuously, providing teams with a customer sentiment layer between formal brand-tracking waves.
Costs range from low monthly survey tools to custom enterprise programs:
Brand tracking should usually sit with brand marketing or growth marketing. Revenue leaders, product marketing, customer success, and PR should feed into the dashboard because brand perception affects pipeline, retention, category position, and customer trust.
Yes, once the company has enough market activity to create public signals. Brand monitoring catches live brand mentions, sentiment spikes, and AI visibility changes. A brand tracker measures whether those signals shift awareness, consideration, preference, and brand loyalty .
ROI comes from connecting brand movement to business outcomes. Track brand metrics beside campaign spend, branded search, direct traffic, conversion rate, pipeline, win rate, retention, and customer feedback.
HubSpot AEO helps connect the dots by showing where the brand appears in answer engines, which prompts cite competitors, and which recommendations can improve visibility. For teams on Marketing Hub Pro or Enterprise, HubSpot AEO also layers in CRM data, so teams can connect AI visibility to the campaigns and contacts driving pipeline.
Brand tracking in 2026 has moved beyond quarterly awareness charts. The strongest teams now combine structured surveys, brand monitoring, customer feedback, social listening, search demand, AI visibility, and CRM reporting. It’s likely teams will need a few tools from the list, at least for social listening and AI visibility.
HubSpot AEO is the most relevant addition to the brand monitoring stack for teams looking to understand how the brand appears in answer engines, which prompts create visibility gaps, and which sources influence the answers.
Pair it with HubSpot Customer Feedback Software and attribution reporting, and brand measurement becomes more useful to revenue teams because it connects market perception, customer sentiment, and campaign performance, so decision leaders can act on the data right away.
And for small teams sharpening their brand foundation, HubSpot’s Free Brand Building Guide is a practical place to start.

title: Scrunch vs. Peec AI: Which tool fits your AEO strategy? [2026]
content:
If you’re comparing Scrunch versus Peec AI , you need to know your buyers are already forming opinions about your brand in answer engines like ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Google AI Mode before they ever reach your website.
Furthermore, if you don’t know how your brand appears in those answers, or if it appears at all, you won’t be able to best optimize your content for a channel that is increasingly shaping first impressions.
Scrunch and Peec AI are two of the most-evaluated AEO platforms for solving the challenge of AEO optimization. Both track brand visibility across AI engines . But they’re built around different assumptions about what your team actually needs.
To help you determine which AEO platform is best for you and your team, this guide compares the features, methodology, exports, use cases, and risks of Scrunch Peec AI.
The right tool fits how your team works, from your reporting cadence to your technical maturity, and what you need to do with the data once you have it.
Scrunch fits your existing stack investment if you are a CMO or VP of Marketing who needs AI visibility as part of a board-level narrative and wants that visibility tied to a DXP like Sitecore or a CMS workflow. However, if you want a clean, standalone tracking and stakeholder reporting without enterprise procurement, Peec AI is the faster option.
If you are an SEO lead or content strategist who needs daily prompt-level tracking, engine coverage across the most-used answer engines, and a reporting layer you can bring to clients or internal stakeholders without design work, Peec AI is the more purpose-built choice.
Scrunch’s brand narrative and descriptor analysis is the best solution if you are a PR or brand manager tracking how AI engines characterize your brand.
If you are a RevOps or marketing ops lead who needs clean data exports, Looker Studio connectors, or API/MCP integrations for attribution reporting, Peec AI’s Advanced plan and Scrunch’s native Looker integration both serve this workflow.
If your team is new to AEO and is still validating whether AI visibility tracking belongs in the budget, Peec AI’s Starter tier ($95/month, unlimited users, daily tracking) is the lower-risk entry point.
If your team is mature in AEO and runs on Sitecore or is evaluating a DXP , Scrunch increasingly makes sense as the combined platform deepens. Still, teams should evaluate the integration roadmap before assuming feature parity with the standalone product.
Pro tip: The most common evaluation mistake teams make is choosing a tool based on engine count. What matters more is whether the tool measures those engines in a methodologically consistent way and whether the output maps to your reporting needs. A tool that covers six engines with API-based sampling and one that covers three engines with front-end monitoring will give you very different data.
What we like: Peec AI’s unlimited-user model across all tiers is unusual in this category. Most AEO platforms charge per seat, which makes team cost hard to predict as you add stakeholders. Scrunch’s per-user fee structure on lower tiers adds up quickly for teams with more than three or four collaborators.
Branded versus non-branded prompts: Scrunch’s default prompt library skews toward brand-name queries. Peec AI lets you build a custom prompt library from scratch, which is important for teams tracking non-branded category prompts where your brand might appear without being named — a common AEO misstep.
Sitewide versus page analysis: Scrunch analyzes individual pages. For teams that want to understand how the full content architecture influences AI citation patterns, this creates gaps that sitewide tools like Profound address more completely.
Update cadence: Peec AI’s daily tracking matters for teams in competitive or fast-moving categories where a week-old snapshot misses meaningful shifts. Scrunch’s weekly export model is fine for strategic narrative monitoring but less suited to operational response cycles.
Before comparing the tools on methodology, it helps to share a plain-language grounding in the terms that matter for AEO evaluation; for a broader reference, see our artificial intelligence glossary for marketers.
AEO (Answer Engine Optimization): The practice of optimizing content and brand presence so that AI systems — ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, Google AI Mode — accurately include, cite, and frame your brand when answering relevant queries.
AI Visibility: A measure of how frequently, and how favorably, an AI system names or cites your brand in response to relevant prompts. It is less about position (like traditional SEO rank) and more about inclusion, attribution, and framing.
AI Overview: Google’s AI-generated summary that appears at the top of some search results pages. Appearing in an AI Overview is different from ranking in the ten blue links — it requires a different approach to content and structure.
Entity: In the context of AI search, an entity is a clearly defined, recognizable concept — a brand, a person, a product, a category — that AI systems can confidently identify and reference. Strong entity definition improves the likelihood of accurate, consistent citation.
Citation: When an AI system references or links to a specific piece of content as the source for a claim in its answer. Citations are the mechanism through which AI search drives referral traffic and brand visibility.
The single most important question to ask of any AEO tool is: How does it collect data?
API-based sampling queries AI engines through their developer APIs, which return different results than the consumer-facing interfaces most of your audience actually uses. API responses may omit citations, surface different content, and behave differently from what a real user experiences. Several practitioners have flagged this on forums like r/GrowthHacking, warning that “API calls ... turned out to be either missing or not real.”
Front-end monitoring replicates what actual users see by querying AI engines through their consumer interfaces. This produces more realistic citation and framing data but is more resource-intensive for platforms to operate.
Both Scrunch and Peec AI have been somewhat opaque about their exact methodology, which is itself worth noting. When evaluating either tool, ask your sales contact directly: How do you collect this data? Is it API-based or front-end? How do you account for personalization variance?
Personalization variance is a real caveat for all tools in this category. AI engines personalize responses based on user history, location, and session context. Any tool that runs prompts from a shared infrastructure will produce a reading that may differ from what your specific audience sees. Treat all AI visibility scores as directional signals, not exact metrics.
Sampling and cadence bias: Peec AI’s daily cadence reduces the risk that a weekly snapshot misses a meaningful change in AI answer patterns. Scrunch’s weekly export model is adequate for narrative monitoring but should not be used for operational response cycles.
Benchmark consistency: When comparing two tools’ outputs for the same brand, you will almost certainly see different numbers. Engine selection, query phrasing, and measurement methodology all affect scores. The goal is not to find the “true” number — it is to track your own trend over time within a single consistent tool.
Try the HubSpot AEO Grader to benchmark your brand’s current AI visibility before choosing a tracking platform. Understanding your baseline helps you evaluate which tool’s reporting maps most closely to your actual position.
How data gets out of a tool often matters more than how it gets in. If your team’s reporting stack runs through Looker Studio, your BI tool, or a RevOps dashboard, export and integration constraints will shape your actual workflow more than any dashboard feature.
What we like: Scrunch’s Looker Studio integration has been called out positively by practitioners on r/seogrowth, specifically for making AI referral data shareable without customization. If Looker is your primary reporting layer, Scrunch’s native connector has an edge — though Peec AI’s Advanced plan now closes this gap.
For teams that need to communicate AI visibility results to leadership or clients, both tools produce dashboards that can be screenshotted or shared via link. Scrunch’s report outputs have been specifically praised for client-readiness without design work. Peec AI’s dashboard is clean and scannable for internal stakeholder review.
For executive reporting , the most important thing is not the export format — it is the framing. AI visibility metrics like share of voice, sentiment trend, and citation source authority need a short narrative layer before they land in a board deck. Neither tool automates that narrative; that work still lives with your team.
This is where the tools diverge most sharply for mid-sized teams.
Peec AI includes unlimited users across all tiers. A 10-person marketing team pays the same $95/month as a 2-person team at the Starter level. As you add stakeholders from PR, RevOps, or agency partners, the cost remains the same.
Scrunch’s Starter plan includes 3 user licenses. The Growth and Enterprise tiers allow more seats, but per-user scaling still applies. For a 10-15 person team, this can push effective monthly costs well above the headline price.
For agencies managing multiple brands, both tools offer agency-specific pricing tracks. Verify current terms with each vendor, as pricing has shifted with Scrunch’s post-acquisition transition.
Recommended reporting cadence: Weekly for operational tracking and content team briefs. Monthly for competitive trend analysis and stakeholder reporting. Quarterly for strategic audit and prompt library refresh.
The most useful way to choose between these tools is to match your primary use case to the platform best suited to it.
Best fit: Scrunch. If your primary question is “How is AI describing our brand — what words, what framing, what sentiment?” Scrunch’s brand descriptor and narrative tracking are the most developed in this category. Independent reviewers consistently rate it highest for sentiment-tracking precision, noting that it captures not just whether a brand appears but also how it is characterized relative to competitors. For PR teams managing message consistency across AI ecosystems, this is the clearest value proposition.
Best fit: Peec AI for self-serve teams; enterprise platforms like Profound for teams needing the broadest coverage. Peec AI covers ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Google AI Mode, with plans to expand; for a deeper dive into Perplexity’s capabilities and market position, see our guide to the platform .
Partial fit for both; full optimization elsewhere. Both tools identify content gaps — prompts or topics where competitors are cited, and you are not. However, neither Scrunch nor Peec AI closes the loop from gap identification to content brief generation to the extent that platforms like Profound or ZipTie do. If content optimization workflow automation is the primary need, plan to supplement either tool or evaluate purpose-built optimization platforms alongside them.
Best fit: Peec AI for structured competitive benchmarking; Scrunch for narrative comparison. Peec’s share-of-voice analysis across engines gives content and RevOps teams clear competitive positioning data. Scrunch’s competitor language comparison helps PR teams understand whether a competitor’s AI framing is improving relative to yours.
A useful frame for evaluating any AEO tool is where it sits in the monitoring → optimization → activation spectrum:
Both Scrunch and Peec AI primarily fall into the monitoring category, with some optimization signals. Teams that need the full loop — from visibility data to shipped content to attributed outcomes — should plan for a stack that supplements either tool with optimization and activation layers.
Scrunch’s most distinctive and most debated feature is its Agent Experience Platform (AXP) , which reformats existing site content into an AI-readable layer served to AI crawlers at the network edge — without altering the human-facing experience.
The case of Sitecore and Scrunch makes the point that AXP helps AI systems accurately read and cite your content, closing the gap between what you publish and what AI agents extract. The reformatting happens at the CDN layer, so human visitors never see it.
The concerns raised by practitioners are worth taking seriously:
No independent evidence of effectiveness: At the time of writing, there is no peer-reviewed or third-party validated evidence that AXP meaningfully improves AI visibility scores. Scrunch’s visibility in AI search — as measured by Profound’s tracking data — was 4.7% (ranked #23), compared to Profound’s 47.1% (#1). Critics argue that if AXP worked as claimed, Scrunch’s own brand would be a stronger demonstration of that. Scrunch has not published controlled lift studies.
Technical complexity: AXP requires software to route AI traffic. For enterprise teams with existing CDN configurations, this adds infrastructure overhead and a new potential point of failure.
Our neutral take: AXP is an interesting hypothesis, not a proven playbook. Teams with technically conservative IT or legal teams should evaluate it carefully. Teams looking for proven optimization approaches should prioritize content structure, semantic relevance, schema markup, and earned authority — methods that work for both humans and AI systems and carry no compliance ambiguity.
Personalization variance: AI engines personalize results by user, location, and session history. Any tool’s visibility scores represent a sampled, de-personalized estimate — not a precise measurement of what your audience sees.
Prompt over-fitting: Designing prompts specifically around branded queries where you already appear well can inflate visibility scores without reflecting real customer discovery behavior. A healthy prompt library should include non-branded categories, use cases, and comparison queries.
Global index reliance: AI engines use different training data, browsing, and retrieval mechanisms by region. Visibility scores in US English prompts may not reflect performance in other markets.
Making decisions across tools: Because methodology varies, comparing scores across tools is unreliable. Anchor your measurement to a single tool and track trends over time within that tool, rather than chasing an “accurate” absolute number.
Use this 10-step checklist before finalizing either platform. It is designed to surface the workflow and methodology questions that most vendor demos skip.
Step 1: Map your buyer journey to prompt types. Before you set up any tool, list the questions your buyers actually ask at each stage of the journey — awareness, consideration, decision, and retention — using techniques outlined in our buyer journey research guide .
Step 2: Apply branded versus non-branded filters. Most tools weight branded prompt performance heavily by default. Make sure your library includes a meaningful share of non-branded prompts — these are where your category-level authority is being built or lost without you noticing.
Step 3: Segment prompts by persona and journey stage. Tag each prompt with the buyer persona and journey stage it maps to. This enables rollup reporting — “How are we performing for CTO-stage evaluation prompts?” — that connects AI visibility data to pipeline context.
Step 4: Choose prompt tagging conventions before you start. If you plan to roll up data in Looker Studio or a BI tool, agree on your tagging taxonomy before onboarding. Inconsistent tags are the most common reason AI visibility data fails to make it into executive reporting.
Step 5: Ask every vendor for their data collection methodology. Is it API-based, front-end, or hybrid? How do they handle personalization variance? How often do they refresh data? This is a legitimate question that any serious vendor should answer directly.
Step 6: Validate with a spot-check. Run the same three or four prompts in ChatGPT and Perplexity yourself on the day your tool onboards. Compare your manual results to the tool’s first report. Directional alignment is the goal, not an exact match.
Step 7: Map export requirements before you buy. If you need Looker Studio, API, or MCP integrations, confirm which tier unlocks them — and at what cost. Buying the Starter tier and discovering you need Advanced for the export you actually need is a common budget surprise.
Step 8: Set a reporting cadence and stick to it. Weekly prompt-level review for content team briefs. Monthly competitive trend analysis for stakeholder updates. Quarterly strategic prompt library audit to retire stale prompts and add new ones.
Step 9: Identify one content improvement to test per cycle. AI visibility data is only useful if it leads to a change. Each month, pick one underperforming prompt cluster and test a specific content change — a new structured data block, a revised FAQ section, a new source placement in an owned article. Track whether the change moves your visibility score over 30–60 days.
Step 10: Connect visibility to source authority. Look at which third-party sources AI engines are citing when they mention your category. If competitors are being cited from domains you are not appearing on — media coverage, review sites, analyst reports — that is a PR and content activation signal, not just a tracking insight.
Use the HubSpot AEO Grader to audit your current AI visibility baseline before choosing a tool. [ Try AEO Grader → ]
AI visibility data is most valuable when it flows into the systems where content is built, campaigns are launched, and revenue is tracked. A monitoring tool that lives in its own silo is an expensive dashboard. Connected to the right marketing infrastructure, AEO insights become a systematic competitive advantage.
1. AEO Insights (Scrunch or Peec AI): Identify which prompts your brand is winning, losing, or absent from. Flag the third-party sources AI engines are citing. Note how competitors are being framed in relation to you. Flag sentiment shifts.
2. Content Briefs (HubSpot Content Hub) Translate gap data into actionable briefs. A non-branded prompt your competitor owns is a content opportunity — write the piece, add structured data, and build internal links that signal topical authority. HubSpot Content Hub connects your AI visibility gaps directly to a content creation workflow, with HubSpot’s AI tools helping generate drafts grounded in your brand voice and positioning.
3. Activation (HubSpot Marketing Hub) Distribute content across channels — email, social media , paid — with Marketing Hub’s automation layer. For PR teams, the source citations from your AEO data identify the exact publications and domains you need coverage on. Earned media and owned content reinforce each other in AI citation patterns.
4. Attribution (HubSpot Smart CRM) Track which content is driving AI-referred traffic, pipeline, and revenue. HubSpot’s Smart CRM ties contact and deal data back to content touchpoints so that you can move from “our AI visibility score went up” to “we closed $X in deals influenced by AI-referred traffic.”
5. Iteration (HubSpot’s AI tools) Use HubSpot’s AI tools to surface patterns in your CRM and engagement data that point to the next round of AEO improvements. Which content pieces are being cited most? Which buyer personas are arriving from AI search? What questions are they asking when they get to your site?
This loop — Insights → Briefs → Activation → Attribution → Iteration — is what separates teams that use AEO data tactually from teams that build a systematic advantage in AI search.
Ready to connect AI visibility to your revenue stack? [ Get a HubSpot demo → ]
For multi-engine tracking at self-serve pricing, Peec AI has a structural advantage. Its Starter plan covers ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Google AI Mode, with daily tracking, and lets you choose which three engines to prioritize.
Scrunch covers a similar engine list but has historically focused more on brand narrative and descriptor analysis than on cross-engine prompt-level benchmarking. For competitive benchmarking — share-of-voice across engines, framing comparison — Peec AI’s analytics layer is more directly oriented toward that workflow.
For narrative-level competitor comparison (how AI describes your competitor versus you), Scrunch has been the stronger offering.
Start by mapping your buyer journey. Identify the questions buyers ask at awareness (category queries), consideration (use case and feature queries), and decision (comparison and brand queries) stages.
For each stage, create both branded and non-branded variants. Tag each prompt with persona, journey stage, product line, and competitive relevance. Agree on this taxonomy before onboarding — retroactive retagging is difficult in most tools. A prompt library of 50–150 well-tagged prompts will give you more actionable insight than 350 unstructured ones.
Both tools offer CSV exports on all paid plans. Looker Studio integration is available on Scrunch natively and on Peec AI’s Advanced plan ($495/month). API access requires Enterprise on both platforms. Peec AI adds MCP integration at the Enterprise level, which is useful for teams building AI-native reporting or automation workflows.
If Looker Studio is your primary reporting layer and you are on a mid-market budget, Scrunch’s native integration has historically been the more seamless option — though Peec AI’s Advanced plan closes this gap for teams willing to step up to that tier.
Four risks stand out for teams acting on AEO data. First, prompt over-fitting — building a prompt library entirely around branded queries where you already perform well, produces flattering scores that do not reflect real customer discovery. Include non-branded category prompts.
Second, AXP or cloaking-style approaches — any tactic that serves fundamentally different content to AI crawlers than to human users carries compliance risk that is worth evaluating carefully with your SEO and legal team. Third, over-relying on a single tool’s absolute score — because methodology varies across platforms, the number itself is less important than the trend within a single tool over time.
Fourth, treating visibility as an end goal — visibility without connecting to source authority, content quality, and earned media is unlikely to compound. The teams winning in AI search are earning authority, not engineering around it.
The connection requires three things: tagged content, attributed traffic, and a CRM that tracks the full journey. Start by ensuring every piece of content you publish as an AEO response has proper UTM tagging so AI-referred traffic is identifiable in your analytics.
Connect that traffic data to your CRM so you can see which deals touched AI-referred content. Use your AEO tool’s source citation data to identify which third-party domains are driving AI citations for your category — then build a PR and content plan to earn presence on those domains.
Over a 90–180-day cycle, you should be able to draw a line from specific content investments to AI visibility improvements to pipeline influence. HubSpot’s Content Hub, Smart CRM, and Marketing Hub automation are designed to support exactly this loop.
Last updated: July 2026. Scrunch pricing and features reflect those of the standalone product operated prior to the June 2026 Sitecore acquisition; verify current terms directly with Sitecore. Peec AI pricing verified against public sources as of July 2026.

title: Omnichannel customer service: What it is and how to do it
content:
In today’s digital world, customers want to access support quickly via their preferred communication channel. In response, more companies are looking to deliver seamless, personalized support experiences via omnichannel customer service models.
Omnichannel customer service offers flexibility and personalization, which can improve everything from resolution times to overall customer satisfaction rates. In this guide, we’ll explore omnichannel customer service and its benefits, as well as break down how to build an omnichannel service strategy and tips for buying the right omnichannel platform.
Omnichannel customer service is a service strategy designed to create a connected, consistent experience for customers across every communication channel, whether it’s email, live chat, phone, social media , or self-service experiences.
An omnichannel service model ensures that customer history, context, and key data are connected across channels. This approach gives support teams the full context they need to provide faster, more personalized service. Omnichannel service enhances the customer experience by removing the need for customers to repeat themselves and offering the flexibility of starting a conversation on one channel and continuing it on another.
While these terms are often used interchangeably, omnichannel customer service differs from multichannel support.
Multichannel customer service means a business simply offers support through multiple channels, but those channels may operate independently with their own inbox or ticketing queue. Multichannel service offers the convenience of multiple channels for support, but customers often need to repeat information and agents don’t have full conversation history and context when a customer switches channels.
Omnichannel customer service builds upon multichannel support by connecting those channels into a single, unified experience. In omnichannel service, customer conversations, purchase history, previous interactions, and other key context are shared across channels so that agents have a unified view of customer data and customers can continue their conversation without having to start over.
Most modern omnichannel customer service platforms consolidate support requests from each channel into a shared inbox or ticketing queue, giving agents a complete view of each customer’s history to help them continue conversations seamlessly.
CX leaders who implement omnichannel customer service see tangible benefits for both their customers and their support teams. Here is a list of five key benefits of omnichannel customer service in more detail.
According to research from Salesforce , 56% of customers have to re-explain their issue every time they’re transferred to a different person or department. Omnichannel customer service eliminates this friction point by preserving conversation history and customer context across every touchpoint, which reduces friction for the customer when they reach out for support. When context is carried across channels, customers can pick up where they left off and aren’t required to repeat themselves, resulting in a smoother support experience.
When customer context, history, and account information are centralized in an omnichannel customer service platform, agents spend less time looking for previous interaction history and can instead jump right in to helping solve the customer’s problem.
With tools like HubSpot’s Smart CRM , agents have access to a unified customer record that is automatically enriched with data from emails, calls, and the web, giving them full context before every interaction.
A unified conversation timeline reduces context switching and information gathering for service agents. Agents can also better prioritize urgent issues and resolve requests more efficiently, which allows them to handle a larger volume of requests without compromising the quality of support.
Research shows that up to 82% of customers prefer companies to know who they are and anticipate their needs. Omnichannel customer service helps companies meet this need by giving agents a complete view of the customer, including previous purchases, past support interactions, and other key account context.
This type of data enables support agents to tailor their conversations and make personalized recommendations, creating a more meaningful interaction with customers and building trust along the way. When companies layer tools like customer agent into their omnichannel strategy, they can use customer data to personalize agent interactions with things like tailored content, special routing rules, and more.
An omnichannel customer service strategy gives organizations a more holistic picture of how their customers are interacting with them across every support channel. This removes the need to analyze each channel individually and instead allows customer support leaders to surface trends, identify bottlenecks, and spot areas of opportunity across the customer journey . This type of visibility helps CX teams improve workflows, optimize staffing, and quickly address customer pain points before they escalate into bigger issues.
Working from a connected service platform with unified customer data makes customer handoffs between agents a seamless process. Whether a case is transferred or an agent is helping a customer that has switched channels, the receiving agent has immediate access to conversation history and context they need to jump in right away and start helping the customer.
The automatic transfer of important information reduces duplicate work, minimizes miscommunication, and ensures that key context isn’t lost in the handoff process between agents. Service Hub’s omnichannel platform features built-in CRM integration and AI-generated conversation and ticket summaries that make handoffs between reps, teams, and channels seamless.
Having the right platform and features is critical to executing a great omnichannel strategy. Below is a list of key features that make a great omnichannel customer service platform.
A shared inbox, like HubSpot’s Free Shared Inbox for Customer Conversations , consolidates conversations from every channel into a single workspace. This unified view of customer requests allows agents to focus on monitoring one inbox instead of monitoring separate inboxes and applications across channels.
With a unified inbox, siloed communication between channels is eliminated, reducing the chance of duplicate or missed responses. Working from the same shared inbox fosters better collaboration between agents, helps with ticket prioritization, and gives customer service leaders better visibility into the queue health and agent capacity.
Shared CRM data connects service interactions to one customer record, enabling agents to view data such as purchase history, subscription plan details, previous support tickets, and more. This gives agents complete customer context before they respond and allows them to offer quicker, more personalized support.
Intelligent routing automatically sends conversations to the right person or team based on predefined rules or AI-surfaced insights. Routing can be set up to trigger based on product expertise, language, geography, account tier, or channel. AI can help prioritize customer routing based on customer intent, sentiment, or urgency.
When a platform can intelligently route conversations, customers have shorter wait times, tickets aren’t left unassigned, and first-contact resolutions improve by matching customers with the best agent to help them. Customer service leaders also benefit from more balanced workloads across the support team, and this feature helps maintain SLAs as ticket volume grows.
Many omnichannel solutions leverage AI to summarize conversations, draft responses, classify or tag tickets, detect sentiment, recommend content, and automate repetitive tasks for human agents. Artificial intelligence can also power chatbots and AI agents that autonomously resolve issues for customers and surface trends and themes across the customer journey.
AI-powered omnichannel platforms like Service Hub help agents be more efficient by automating repetitive manual work. This accelerates resolution times and enhances satisfaction for customers.
When a knowledge base is built into the omnichannel platform, organizations can easily surface relevant information to customers to help them solve their issues independently. Customer support teams also benefit from connected access to the documentation they need to resolve customer issues, such as FAQs, troubleshooting guides, and how-to articles.
Integrating a knowledge base into the omnichannel service platform means that customers can better self-service and human agents spend less time looking for documentation, improving response times and consistency across agent responses.
Pro tip: Platforms like Service Hub even have knowledge base agents that can turn successful service interactions into self-service content that lives in the knowledge base
For customer service teams, service level agreements (SLAs) are a critical metric that is tracked and measured regularly. Many omnichannel service platforms like Service Hub ’s SLA Management can apply SLAs to tickets automatically and alert teams when an SLA deadline is at risk of being missed. SLA policies can be assigned based on predefined criteria such as the customer tier, ticket priority, issue type, or support channel.
When the platform recognizes that an incoming ticket meets specific SLA criteria, it automatically applies the correct SLA, begins tracking its progress, and alerts the right people where needed. This eliminates manual work for both customer service leaders and support agents, automates ticket prioritization, and helps standardize service delivery.
Omnichannel service platforms include centralized dashboards and reports, like HubSpot’s Service Analytics , that allow customer service leaders to understand how response time, resolution time, customer satisfaction, and ticket volume are performing across channels as well as across the entire customer journey.
This type of cross-channel data helps companies quickly surface and address bottlenecks while also measuring team performance and forecasting staffing needs. Analytics can also reveal customer behavior and channel preferences, empowering companies to invest staffing and resources in the right places.
Security settings that safeguard customer and company data are critical for meeting compliance and regulatory requirements. Omnichannel platforms should offer the most up-to-date permission structure, including:
This helps protect customer information and reserves access to sensitive data. AI-powered platforms should also include data protection controls and transparent AI recommendations in order to protect company data while allowing support reps to understand how the AI reached its conclusions.
When implementing an omnichannel customer service strategy, it’s important to take a few foundational steps before expanding to new channels. Below is a step-by-step guide to launching an omnichannel customer service strategy.
Mapping out the customer journey helps customer service leaders identify every touchpoint in the journey and the channels that customers prefer at each different stage. Customer service leaders should also document common support use cases to understand where customers experience the most friction and identify which interactions could be automated. Outlining the customer journey and common support use cases creates a foundation for each additional step in the omnichannel strategy.
CX pro tip: Don’t forget to include customer feedback in this process, as customers are usually quick to tell you where they are experiencing friction. For example, customers may be using one channel more than the others, but that might be because it’s the only channel that gets them through to a human. Consider feedback and all angles when building out this journey map.
A successful omnichannel strategy relies on complete, unified customer data to connect across channels. Customer success leaders will need to integrate customer data into a centralized platform that connects conversations, purchase history, account information, support interactions, and other key customer context.
A unified customer profile enables agents to work faster and offer personalized support while allowing customers to move between channels without losing context. Platforms like Smart CRM can unify customer information, conversations, and tools to create a single customer record.
CX pro tip: Take the time to provide a talk track for your agents to use when they’re picking up a conversation that’s changed channels. This can help them feel more confident jumping into a new conversation if they have a practiced greeting and segue to use with the customer.
Once customer data is connected, all support channel inquiries should feed into a shared inbox so that every conversation can be managed in a single workspace. Organizations will need to establish routing rules that automatically assign conversations based on factors like issue type, sentiment, customer tier, product expertise, or urgency. With a unified inbox and automated routing capabilities like those in Service Hub , support agents become more efficient and have better visibility into the overall support queue.
CX pro tip: Consider which customers you’d want to provide a different experience and use AI to help you achieve that. I’ve seen some companies set routing rules that fast-track certain customers to the front of the support queue, like those with the highest ARR or those who are at-risk but up for renewal in the next six months.
Organizations should consider launching channels in a phased approach, starting with the channel that their customers prefer or use the most frequently. This is often email, live chat, and phone, but may also be messaging channels or social media, depending on the industry. Customer service leaders should also invest in self-service resources such as knowledge bases , FAQs, AI chatbots or agents, and customer portals, like HubSpot’s Customer Portal in Service Hub.
CS pro tip: Customer communities are another great way to help customers self-service, as they connect customers to each other and foster idea sharing. CSMs, support reps, and other internal team members can also create content and engage with customers in the community.
A great omnichannel strategy uses AI to help make agents more effective, not to replace them. AI in omnichannel support supports intent detection, summarization, and suggested replies. AI can also surface relevant knowledge base articles, tag tickets, and automate repetitive tasks .
With omnichannel customer support automation, agents spend less time doing manual, time-consuming work and spend more time helping customers with complex problems that require a human touch. Customer service leaders should develop playbooks for common support procedures for each channel and include the escalation process, troubleshooting workflows, and communication guidelines. Be sure to also train the team on where AI is assisting them so they can provide feedback along the way.
CS pro tip: AI chatbots and agents are great ways to drive efficiencies with artificial intelligence. HubSpot’s AI tools can summarize conversations, automatically route customers to the right department, and assist human agents with tasks that help expedite resolution times.
Roll out an omnichannel strategy in phases instead of all at once. Begin a pilot with a limited scope, such as a few support channels, customer segments, or support teams. This enables CS leaders to monitor performance and quickly pivot if necessary.
CS leaders should also gather customer feedback and input from agents to identify improvement opportunities. Once workflows are refined and performance goals are being met, organizations can continue to roll out their omnichannel strategy across the organization.
Omnichannel customer service metrics should align to business outcomes and be trackable in customer service software . Below is a list of KPIs to track per channel, as well as a few suggested review cadences.
CS pro tip: I also suggest monitoring the AI feedback score on AI capabilities, which measures how often agents rate AI-generated recommendations, responses, or workflows as helpful. This type of feedback can help quickly identify areas to improve AI accuracy, which in turn helps maintain trust with the agents who are using the AI tools.
When customer service leaders regularly review omnichannel service KPIs, they proactively evaluate performance and stay ahead of issues. While most CS leaders are probably reviewing these metrics daily, below are a few common metric review cadences and the additional stakeholders that are often included in each review.
Weekly metric reviews focus on the day-to-day health of the overall support operation and often monitor operational metrics such as ticket volume, response and resolution times, SLA compliance, queue health, and agent workloads.
These meetings offer the opportunity to identify potential emerging issues as well as adjusting staffing and processes so that small problems don’t balloon into bigger issues. Weekly reviews usually include customer service managers or directors, support team leads, and CX or CS operations members.
Monthly customer journey reviews are an opportunity to evaluate the end-to-end customer experience and look for improvement opportunities. These meetings are higher level than the weekly reviews and offer a broader look at how customers experience support across every channel. CS leaders should analyze customer feedback, CSAT and CES trends, self-service adoption, and channel performance for each part of the customer journey.
These insights can help improve content, optimize AI or workflows, and remove friction or barriers for customers. Monthly customer journey reviews usually include customer service leadership, customer experience leadership, customer education team members, and may also include representation from the digital experience or customer success team.
Quarterly reviews should focus on the long-term strategy to help CS leaders evaluate whether the omnichannel strategy is supporting broader business goals. Often attended by senior directors or VPs from customer service and customer success, the metrics in this cadence should reflect higher-level insights like long-term trends, overall performance, customer insights, and alignment on business priorities.
This kind of review helps the organization determine where investments should be made next, whether it’s expanding to new channels or implementing new AI-driven workflows to help human agents. CS leaders can present a roadmap with priorities and plans for evolving the omnichannel strategy over the next one to two quarters.
When choosing an omnichannel customer service platform, think beyond feature checklists and instead assess how well the platform can support the customer experience strategy over time. Below are five questions that decision-makers can ask themselves to ensure they’re purchasing the best omnichannel service platform for their needs.
The omnichannel platform must support the right channels for your customers. That includes the channel customers are already using the most, the channel customers prefer the most, and other desired communication channels that may be rolled out in the future. It’s also important to make sure the platform supports customers switching between all channels.
Omnichannel strategies rely on unified data, so CS leaders should evaluate if the platform in question can connect customer conversations with CRM records, purchase history, help desk interactions, and other key business systems. It’s also important to make sure that agents will be able to quickly see that history when interacting with customers.
Make sure that the platform that’s chosen meets current needs while supporting future growth. Consider whether the platform supports increasing ticket volume, additional channels, larger teams, and evolving customer expectations. (And if it does support these, ask if there is a cost associated with supporting that growth.)
If a platform lacks strong reporting and analytics, the job of a customer service leader becomes twice as hard. The benefit of an omnichannel platform is the ability to measure metrics across channels, so make sure that the platform in question can easily surface the metrics that the company cares about in a format that is actually usable (i.e. consider the ease of use for dashboards and data visualization tools).
Most customer service platforms include AI, but CS leaders should evaluate whether the AI capabilities align with their overall support strategy. Consider which tasks are best suited for automation and ensure the platform in question provides high-quality AI output, strong data privacy protections, and appropriate AI governance.
Pro tip: Service Hub’s Omnichannel Customer Service makes it easy to scale support across channels, unify customer data, and leverage AI, automation, and analytics to gain key insights.
Many companies see omnichannel implementation take anywhere from a few weeks to several months, though timelines can vary depending on the organization’s size and the complexity of the tech stack. Starting with a smaller pilot and expanding over time can help organizations get started more quickly.
Yes, especially if customers are already reaching out for support across multiple channels. Many omnichannel service platforms are built to scale, making it easy for small teams to start with their existing channels and later expand to new channels as they grow.
Yes, since most omnichannel platforms integrate with popular software tools like CRMs, help desks, and other business tools, it’s possible to unify customer data even with one main system. Once customer data is unified, it’s possible to offer connected support experiences across multiple channels.
Customer service leaders should choose an AI-powered omnichannel platform that uses the same data, conversation history, knowledge base, and workflows that the support team uses. CS leaders should also regularly review AI recommendations and agent feedback to improve accuracy over time. This helps AI become another part of the omnichannel strategy instead of another disconnected tool.
Omnichannel customer service is more than just supporting customers across multiple channels. It’s about using customer context and history to deliver a more personalized, connected experience for customers. Building a successful omnichannel strategy requires preparation, the right technology, and a commitment to ongoing improvement.
Customer service leaders and CX managers looking to implement an omnichannel customer service strategy should consider Service Hub’s Omnichannel Customer Service features. With a unified data ecosystem, multi-channel support capabilities, and the ability to personalize experiences, Service Hub includes everything an organization needs to start or scale their omnichannel customer service strategy.

title: CRM change management: A practical guide for leaders
content:
CRM projects don’t fail at the technical level — they fail because the people expected to use the system never bought in, the training was too generic to stick, and nobody owned adoption after go-live. The result is a CRM that costs money to maintain but doesn’t deliver the pipeline visibility or process alignment it was supposed to.
Getting change management CRM implementation right means addressing the people and process challenges before, during, and after launch, not just configuring the software.
This guide covers the CRM change management strategy, team structure, communication plan, and adoption metrics that turn a CRM deployment into a system teams actually use.
CRM change management is the process of helping teams adopt new CRM tools, workflows, and data standards with enough structure, communication, and training that adoption actually sticks. Most CRM implementations don’t fail because of bad software. They fail because the human side is treated as an afterthought.
The data on structured change management is clear. Prosci’s research across 2,600 change practitioners found that projects with excellent change management meet or exceed their objectives at nearly twice the rate of those with poor change management.
That gap is driven by how well the human side of the rollout is planned and executed.
A well-managed CRM rollout produces three compounding benefits:
The cost of skipping structured change management compounds quickly. Reps revert to spreadsheets. Data degrades. Validity’s 2025 State of CRM Data Management report found that 76% of organizations say less than half their CRM data is accurate and complete. Managers lose pipeline visibility, and within six months leadership is questioning whether the CRM investment was worth it.
Pro tip: For a broader look at change management frameworks, see our overview of change management .
A CRM change management plan is the operational document that ties your rollout together. It should cover seven core elements: readiness assessment, scope definition, goals, stakeholders, timeline, risk log, and success metrics.
Without all seven of these core elements, you are likely to encounter mid-rollout surprises that slow adoption or derail governance.
Two frameworks show up repeatedly in successful CRM rollouts: the Prosci ADKAR model and Kotter’s 8-step process . Neither is mandatory, but both offer useful scaffolding.
ADKAR stands for Awareness, Desire, Knowledge, Ability, and Reinforcement. It’s an individual-focused framework that helps change leaders diagnose exactly where adoption is breaking down. If a rep knows what the CRM is for (Awareness) but doesn’t believe it helps them (Desire), that is a different problem than a rep who wants to use it but doesn’t know how (Knowledge). ADKAR’s diagnostic value is its strongest feature. It turns “people are not adopting” into a specific, addressable gap.
Pro tip: Run a quick ADKAR self-assessment survey with pilot users before your full rollout. Ask each person to rate their Awareness, Desire, Knowledge, Ability, and Reinforcement on a scale of 1 to 5. A score below 3 on any element is your intervention point. This takes about 15 minutes and saves weeks of guesswork.
Kotter’s 8-step model operates at the organizational level: create urgency, build a coalition, form a strategic vision, communicate it, remove obstacles, generate short-term wins, sustain acceleration, and anchor change in culture.
For enterprise CRM rollouts across multiple regions or business units, the coalition-building and urgency steps are particularly relevant. Without visible executive sponsorship, adoption requests read as optional.
My recommendation: use ADKAR to diagnose individual-level gaps and run targeted interventions, and use Kotter’s framing to structure your leadership and communication strategy at the organizational level. The two complement each other well.
CRM change management improves user adoption when the right people are accountable for the right outcomes. A CRM change team includes leaders from marketing, sales, service, operations, IT, enablement, and analytics. The specific roles and responsibilities need to be formalized before launch, not decided on the fly.
The table below shows a practical RACI assignment for a mid-size CRM rollout.
Manage plan, track milestones, coordinate workstreams
Drive rep adoption, reinforce pipeline hygiene norms
Configure system, govern data standards, monitor dashboards
Design and deliver role-based training, office hours
SSO, permissions, integrations, compliance requirements
Lead-to-revenue mapping, campaign-to-CRM workflow adoption
Ticket workflow adoption, CSAT and case resolution standards
Adapt the RACI role assignments to your org structure based on your specific team composition. What matters is that every role and responsibility in your change management plan has a clear accountable owner.
Governance cadences should be established before go-live and maintained post-launch. A weekly adoption stand-up for the first 90 days, a monthly steering committee review through the first year, and a quarterly data governance audit form a reasonable starting cadence.
Clear change communications explain what is changing, what isn’t changing, and why it matters. They do this across multiple channels, for multiple audiences, at multiple points in the rollout. A single launch email isn’t a communication strategy.
Start with an audience message map. Revenue operations leaders, sales reps, service agents, and marketing managers each need a different version of the same core message. A rep cares about whether the CRM makes their day easier. A service lead cares about CSAT visibility and SLA tracking. A RevOps leader cares about pipeline hygiene and forecast accuracy. Write the message for each audience, not one generic version for all.
The “What’s Changing / What’s Not Changing” tracker is one of the highest-value, lowest-effort communication tools available. A simple two-column table shared early in the rollout reduces anxiety, focuses attention on actual workflow changes, and prevents the rumor cycle that forms when people don’t know what to expect.
For communication cadence, use a layered approach: a kick-off announcement from the executive sponsor, team-level briefings from managers, and reinforcement via Slack or email from the CRM program lead. Our guide to communication strategy has additional structure for multi-channel communication planning.
On training: role-based training reduces resistance to CRM adoption because it respects people’s time. A sales rep doesn’t need to understand how ticketing works. A service agent doesn’t need deal pipeline configuration training. Training that feels irrelevant creates resistance. Training that maps directly to daily workflow creates confidence.
The most effective training architectures combine four layers:
HubSpot Academy offers free certification courses in HubSpot CRM , Sales Hub , Service Hub , and Marketing Hub that can be assigned to teams as part of a structured enablement plan. These are particularly useful for onboarding new hires post-rollout.
Pro tip: Build a training completion dashboard before go-live. Track which users have completed which modules, and give managers visibility into their team’s training status. Completion rates drop sharply when nobody is watching them. When managers see the numbers, they follow up.
Feedback loops belong in the communication plan, not as an afterthought. Pulse surveys at 30, 60, and 90 days give you early warning on adoption problems before they become entrenched habits. Anonymous feedback forms capture what users wouldn’t say in a group setting. Both are easier to act on than trying to diagnose low adoption rates after the fact.
Most CRM rollout failures are predictable. These are the patterns that derail otherwise well-planned implementations, along with the steps that prevent or remediate each one.
When nobody owns adoption measurement, nobody is accountable for low adoption. This shows up as diffused responsibility: IT thinks sales owns training, sales thinks IT owns configuration, and RevOps is caught in the middle. Preventive step: assign a named CRM program lead with a defined scope of authority before the project kicks off. If you are mid-rollout and ownership is unclear, run a rapid RACI mapping workshop to establish it immediately.
Executive sponsors who announce the CRM at launch and then disappear send an unintentional signal: this is optional. Prosci’s research across 2,600 change practitioners found that projects with good change management programs meet or exceed objectives at a 73% rate, versus 39% for fair programs. The difference in visible, sustained leadership advocacy is a primary driver of that gap. Preventive step: build regular CRM updates into existing leadership forums like QBRs, all-hands meetings, and leadership reviews.
One-size-fits-all CRM training wastes everyone’s time and signals that the rollout team did not think carefully about actual user workflows. Preventive step: design training tracks by role before go-live. If you are already past launch, survey frontline users on what they still don’t know how to do, then run targeted micro-sessions on those specific gaps.
Every unnecessary field, every redundant workflow, every custom object that doesn’t map to a real process is a maintenance burden and an adoption friction point. I have watched CRM instances with 400+ custom properties become unusable within 18 months because nobody governed what went in. Preventive step: establish a field request process with a required business case before any new property is added. For existing instances, run a property audit and archive anything unused in the last 90 days.
Bad data produces bad reports, bad reports erode trust in the system, and low trust produces low adoption. Validity’s 2025 research shows 76% of organizations have inaccurate CRM data , which means governance that starts weak gets worse fast. Preventive step: define required fields, data entry standards, and a duplicate management protocol before go-live. Our guides on data hygiene and CRM data maintenance cover the specific practices in depth.
Rollouts that treat feedback as a PR exercise by collecting it but not acting on it destroy adoption trust faster than any technical problem. Preventive step: establish a documented feedback review cycle and communicate what you are doing with the input. If you have collected feedback without visible action, run a “you said, we did” communication to rebuild credibility before the next review cycle.
